summary: Assert/error inventory of the machine API layers (C API, Lua bindings, JSON-RPC server and client, json-util, base64/hex, local-machine, i-machine). Every path that carries other parties' data (input payloads through send/log/verify_send_cmio_response, guest-declared tx-buffer lengths through receive_cmio_request, access logs and hashes through the verify_* functions, chain hex through cartesi.fromhex) was found bounded and error-reporting: no assert, abort, exit, unchecked index or data-sized allocation reachable from such data was found. One Low-rated candidate is reported for completeness; no candidate at Medium or above.

candidates.title: base64 and hex decoders throw from inside std::string::resize_and_overwrite, which the C++ standard leaves undefined, on malformed data from other parties
candidates.component: base64.hpp decode_base64 / hex.hpp decode_hex (used by json-util from_json of hashes and access logs, the JSON-RPC server handlers, and the Lua cartesi.frombase64/fromhex/fromjson)
candidates.role: Support for the verify paths and Lua helpers; the same decoders also parse the JSON-RPC server's send_cmio_response data and the C API's JSON arguments, which the honest operator uses (honest-operator role where a production node calls them)
candidates.location: src/base64.hpp decode_base64 (op passed to resize_and_overwrite calls decode_base64_digits, which throws std::domain_error/std::invalid_argument on invalid characters, padding or length); src/hex.hpp decode_hex (op calls decode_hex_digits, which throws std::domain_error on a non-hex digit)
candidates.description: Both decoders size the output string with resize_and_overwrite and validate the input inside the operation, so malformed input makes the operation throw. The standard leaves a throwing operation of resize_and_overwrite undefined. libstdc++ (the supported Linux toolchain) resets the length through a scope guard, so nothing goes wrong there. libc++ leaves the string at length n with uninitialized bytes until it is destroyed. The callers discard the string on that path, so the uninitialized bytes are never read in practice.
candidates.trigger: Any party whose bytes reach these decoders: a claimant's access log or hash in base64 (verify_* through Lua, the C API or JSON-RPC), relayed chain data in hex (cartesi.fromhex in the bridge), or an input payload in base64 on the JSON-RPC send_cmio_response path (bytes the honest node encodes itself, so malformed only through a node bug).
candidates.reachability: Reachable with malformed data from other parties on the verify and Lua helper paths. Observed behavior on this build (libstdc++): a clean exception that becomes an error return (cartesi.frombase64('QUJD@===') and cartesi.fromhex('0x4g') fail under pcall, with no crash).
candidates.rating_steps: 1. Out of scope? No exclusion applies to the trigger: the data comes from other parties and reaches the API through a trusted caller (section 8, 'Data from other parties that a trusted caller passes through it stays in scope'). 2. Role: a library. It 'stands in for the most critical role among the components that reach the defect through it' (section 3). That includes the C API JSON parsing on the honest operator's path. 3. High/Medium cases: none matches. No crash, hang, memory-safety defect or unbounded allocation is observed or expected on the supported toolchain: libstdc++ defines the outcome, and libc++ leaves only unread uninitialized bytes in a discarded string. 4. Critical: section 4 says these paths 'must be memory-safe and bounded, and must report errors without terminating the process'. On supported hosts they do, so no rule is violated in effect. R1's 'Undefined behavior' clause concerns transitions, which this code does not compute. 5. Low: a real defect, undefined behavior per the language standard, that violates no rule in effect.
candidates.threat_to_goal: None on the supported toolchain. It is latent: a standard library that relied on the precondition, for example by asserting or terminating in a hardened mode, could turn malformed relayed data into a process abort on the honest operator's API path. That would be a crash caused by data from other parties.
candidates.evidence: Code reading of base64.hpp, base64.cpp, hex.hpp and hex.cpp, and the libstdc++ 13 resize_and_overwrite implementation (/usr/include/c++/13/bits/basic_string.tcc:574-604, _Terminator guard). Lua probe on the in-tree build: pcall(cartesi.frombase64,'QUJD@===') -> false, pcall(cartesi.fromhex,'0x4g') -> false, with no crash.
candidates.test_idea: A unit test that builds the decoders with a hardened libc++ (_LIBCPP_HARDENING_MODE=_LIBCPP_HARDENING_MODE_DEBUG) or under a checker that flags a throwing resize_and_overwrite operation, feeds malformed base64 and hex, and asserts a clean exception. The fix is to validate the input, or decode into a local buffer, before resize_and_overwrite, or to make the operation return 0 and raise the error after it.

checked_without_candidate: cm.cpp: every entry point is a function-try-block that maps every exception to an error code (cm-exception.hpp maps every standard exception type plus unknown). Null-pointer checks exist on outputs. cm_send/log/verify_send_cmio_response take uint32 lengths. Hashes are memcpy'd from fixed-size cm_hash. Temporary strings are thread-local.

machine::receive_cmio_request clamps the guest-declared length to the tx buffer. The C API, the Lua binding (local length query, then resize; remote worst case of 2 MiB) and the JSON-RPC server (vector sized min(max_length, TX_LEN)) and client (consistency checks on available_length and data size) are bounded.

send_cmio_response: an oversized input is a no-op that never reads data. The JSON-RPC client replaces oversized data with rx_len+1 zero bytes, which keeps the no-op and the same log. Lua and JSON-RPC reject lengths above UINT32_MAX. check_cmio_response_revert_root_hash checks the same yield condition as send_cmio_response.

json-util: integer conversions are range-checked (uint16/uint32/int32/uint8). machine_hash requires exactly 32 decoded bytes. Access log parsing bounds log2_size to INT_MAX and checks note/bracket counts. The replay checks size, address, sibling count and data (replay-send-cmio-state-access.hpp, access::make_proof) before the assert-only get_word_access_data/replace_word_access_data.

JSON-RPC server: dispatch catches everything and turns it into an error response. A NUL byte and nesting depth over 256 are rejected. Non-UTF-8 results are replaced by an error. Fork closes the parent's sessions in the child with close(), not shutdown(), kills a forked child whose response cannot be sent, and refuses shared backing stores. Rebind and shutdown were reviewed.

JSON-RPC client: response id, jsonrpc, error and result validation, depth limit, and socket close on any error. Timeout semantics are documented in cm-jsonrpc.h (the state is unknown after a timeout). The PRT recipes never set a timeout.

Lua bindings: allocation failures are reported as errors. Managed to-be-closed slots hold all C++ objects across luaL_error, so no non-trivial C++ destructor is skipped by longjmp in the methods reviewed (clua-i-machine.cpp, clua-cartesi.cpp, clua-cartesi-jsonrpc.cpp). Schema-driven JSON<->Lua conversion is depth-limited. Break-reason name maps match the C enums and interpret.hpp.
local-machine.cpp and i-machine.hpp: thin forwarding with a 'no machine' check, and nothing more.
not_covered: No fuzzing or ASan run of the JSON-RPC server handlers over the wire. Only code reading, plus a small Lua probe of the decoders.
clua-cartesi-filesystem.cpp and the cm_filesystem_* C functions: only skimmed (operator-local files, no other-party data).
cartesi/*.lua helpers: hash-tree.lua frontier and forest functions beyond verify_slice, verify_splice and get_data_root_hash. evmu.lua, gdbstub.lua and bash.lua were not reviewed.
jsonrpc-discover.cpp and the discover JSON schema were not compared with the handlers.
Behavior of the JSON-RPC client and server under libc++/macOS (fork, OpenMP pause, posix_spawn flags) was not tested.
Machine-core behavior behind the API (collect_* internals, the hash tree, store/load/clone) was left to other angles. Only its API-visible preconditions were checked.

Exception safety of the JSON-RPC server when serializing very large successful results (std::bad_alloc in j.dump() escapes handle_request and ends the server process through main's catch). It is reachable only with caller-chosen sizes or memory exhaustion (a host fault), so it is not reported.
cm_jsonrpc_fork_server leaks the forked server process if constructing the client object throws after the fork succeeded. Only bad_alloc can cause this, so it is not reported.
